'''Jacek K. Furdyna''' (September 6, 1933 – September 28, 2026) was a Polish-American physicist and academic. He was a Professor Emeritus at the [[University of Notre Dame]].<ref name=gpq>{{Cite web|url=https://physics.nd.edu/people/jacek-furdyna/|title=Jacek Furdyna|first=Marketing Communications|last= Notre Dame|website=Department of Physics and Astronomy}}</ref>

Furdyna is most known for his publications in [[condensed matter physics]], and particularly for his research on elemental and compound semiconductors, in which he explored various [[Electromagnetism|electromagnetic phenomena]], including magnetoplasma effects such as [[Helicon (physics)|helicon wave]] propagation,<ref name=qqq>{{cite journal |last1=Palik |first1=E D |last2=Furdyna |first2=J K |title=Infrared and microwave magnetoplasma effects in semiconductors |journal=Reports on Progress in Physics |date=1 September 1970 |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=1193–1322 |doi=10.1088/0034-4885/33/3/307 |bibcode=1970RPPh...33.1193P }}{{primary source inline|date=January 2025}}</ref><ref name=edc>{{cite journal |last1=Surma |first1=M. |last2=Furdyna |first2=J. K. |last3=Praddaude |first3=H. C. |title=Alfvén-Wave Propagation in Pyrolytic and Single-Crystal Graphite |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=14 December 1964 |volume=13 |issue=24 |pages=710–712 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.710 |bibcode=1964PhRvL..13..710S }}{{primary source inline|date=January 2025}}</ref><ref name=wsx>{{cite journal |last1=Furdyna |first1=Jacek K. |title=Helicons, Magnetoplasma Edge, and Faraday Rotation in Solid State Plasmas at Microwave Frequencies |journal=Applied Optics |date=1 April 1967 |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=675–684 |doi=10.1364/AO.6.000675 |pmid=20057824 |bibcode=1967ApOpt...6..675F }}{{primary source inline|date=January 2025}}</ref> [[Magneto-optic effect|magneto-optics]],<ref name=whoosh>{{cite journal |last1=Oh |first1=Eunsoon |last2=Ramdas |first2=A.K. |last3=Furdyna |first3=J.K. |title=Magneto-optic phenomena in II–VI diluted magnetic semiconductors: the Faraday and the Voigt effect |journal=Journal of Luminescence |date=June 1992 |volume=52 |issue=1–4 |pages=183–191 |doi=10.1016/0022-2313(92)90243-3 |bibcode=1992JLum...52..183O }}{{primary source inline|date=January 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tulchinsky |first1=D. In recognition of his research, he has been awarded [[Honorary degree|honorary doctorates]] by [[University of Warsaw]] and [[Purdue University]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.purdue.edu/uns/x/2007a/07hondocs/07Furdyna.html|title=2007 Honorary Degree|website=www.purdue.edu}}</ref> as well as The Nicholas Copernicus Medal from the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]] for his significant contributions in designing and developing novel [[List of semiconductor materials|semiconductor materials]], including [[magnetic semiconductor]]s intended to perform advanced functions in computer technology.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://science.nd.edu/news-and-media/news/furdyna-awarded-copernicus-medal-by-polish-academy-of-sciences/|title=Furdyna Awarded Copernicus Medal by Polish Academy of Sciences|first=Marissa|last=Gebhard|website=College of Science|date=20 July 2009 }}</ref>

He was Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], the [[Nanovic Institute for European Studies]] at Notre Dame,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nanovic.nd.edu/news/faculty-fellow-invited-to-join-ukrainian-journal-of-physics-international-advisory-board/|title=Faculty Fellow invited to join Ukrainian Journal of Physics International Advisory Board|first=Jennifer|last=Lechtanski|website=Nanovic Institute|date=3 December 2010 }}</ref> and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].

==Early life and education==
Furdyna was born on September 6, 1933, in Kamionka Strumiłowa, Poland (now Kamianka Buzka, Ukraine). After invasion of Poland by the Soviet Union in 1939 at the outset of [[World War II]], he was deported to Siberia with his mother, while his father was taken to the Gulag north of the Polar Circle. When war broke out between Nazi Germany and USSR, Polish deportees (including him among them) were formally "amnestied", and in 1942 many of them were able to evacuate from the Soviet Union through Uzbekistan to Iran, where he started attending elementary school in Teheran. He then traveled through Iraq, with short stays in Baghdad and Kirkuk, to (then) Palestine, where he was able to continue his education. In 1947 he and his mother joined his father in the United Kingdom, and at the age of 15 he immigrated with his parents to the United States, settling in Chicago in 1948.<ref>{{cite book |last=Mycielska-Dowgiałło |first= Elżbieta |date=2012 |title= Ci, o których powinniśmy pamiętać|url= |location= |publisher=Szkoła Wyższa Przymierza Rodzin |pages=91–153 |isbn=978-83-61140-33-7}}</ref>
 
He earned his BS degree in [[Physics]] from [[Loyola University Chicago]] in 1955, followed by his Ph.D. from [[Northwestern University]] in 1960<ref name=gpq/> under the supervision of Sybrand Broersma. The title of his doctoral thesis was "Faraday Effect in Silicon and Germanium".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Furdyna |first1=J. K. |last2=Broersma |first2=S. |title=Microwave Faraday Effect in Silicon and Germanium |journal=Physical Review |date=15 December 1960 |volume=120 |issue=6 |pages=1995–2003 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.120.1995 |bibcode=1960PhRv..120.1995F }}{{primary source inline|date=January 2025}}</ref>

==Career==
After earning his Ph.D. in experimental [[solid-state physics]], Furdyna spent two years as postdoctoral fellow at Northwestern's Department of Electrical Engineering before joining the staff of the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|M.I.T.]] Francis Bitter National Magnet Laboratory from 1962 to 1966. He then joined the Physics Department at Purdue University in 1966 as associate professor, and was promoted to Professor of Physics in 1972. His other notable appointments include being the [[National Academy of Sciences]] Exchange Scholar at the Institute of Physics of Polish Academy of Sciences and at Warsaw University from 1972 to 1973, a Visiting Scholar at the [[National Research Council Canada]] in [[Ottawa]] in 1981, and the Director of the [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] Materials Research Laboratory at Purdue University from 1982 to 1985. He held an appointment as the Aurora and Thomas Marquez Chair of [[Information Theory]] and Computer Technology in the Department of Physics at the University of Notre Dame from 1987 until 2021, and has been a Professor Emeritus of Physics since that time.<ref name=gpq/>

==Research==
Furdyna was the author or co-author of over 900 publications<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=XyjUQPAAAAAJ&hl=en|title=Jacek K. Furdyna|website=scholar.google.com}}</ref> in the field of semiconductor physics, most of his later research activity focusing on magnetic semiconductors, their nanostructures, and their spintronic applications.<ref name=hjh>{{cite journal |last1=Furdyna |first1=J. K. |title=Diluted magnetic semiconductors: An interface of semiconductor physics and magnetism (invited) |journal=Journal of Applied Physics |date=November 1982 |volume=53 |issue=11 |pages=7637–7643 |doi=10.1063/1.330137 |bibcode=1982JAP....53.7637F }}{{primary source inline|date=January 2025}}</ref><ref name=DMS>{{cite journal |last1=Furdyna |first1=J. K. |title=Diluted magnetic semiconductors |journal=Journal of Applied Physics |date=15 August 1988 |volume=64 |issue=4 |pages=R29–R64 |doi=10.1063/1.341700 }}{{primary source inline|date=January 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1002/3527600434.eap420 |chapter=Semiconductors, Diluted Magnetic |title=Digital Encyclopedia of Applied Physics |date=2003 |last1=Furdyna |first1=J. K. |last2=Dobrowolska |first2=M. |last3=Luo |first3=H. |isbn=978-3-527-26841-2 }}{{primary source inline|date=January 2025}}</ref> His earlier interests included the physics of blue-green laser<ref>{{cite journal|first2=J.K.|last2=Furdyna|first1=H.|last1=Luo|journal= Semiconductor Science and Technology|volume= 10|page=1041|date=1995|title=The II- VI semiconductor blue-green laser: challenges and solution|issue=8 |doi=10.1088/0268-1242/10/8/001|bibcode=1995SeScT..10.1041L |s2cid=250921117 }}</ref> and electromagnetic wave propagation in conducting solids, including extensive studies of helicon waves, Alfven waves, and related plasma effects in semiconductors and semimetals.<ref name=qqq/><ref name=edc/><ref name=wsx/>

He made contributions in several fields of semiconductor physics. In his early work he explored the interaction of [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic waves]] with free-carrier plasmas in these materials, particularly in the presence of external [[magnetic field]]s. This included studies of microwave [[Faraday effect]] and a series of magneto-plasma phenomena, such as helicon and Alfven waves, [[Cyclotron motion#Cyclotron resonance|cyclotron resonance]], and various dimensional resonances in semiconductors.<ref name=qqq/><ref name=edc/><ref name=wsx/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dixon |first1=Joseph R. |last2=Furdyna |first2=Jacek K. |title=Microwave helicon resonances in n -InSb spheres |journal=Journal of Applied Physics |date=July 1980 |volume=51 |issue=7 |pages=3762–3771 |doi=10.1063/1.328165 |bibcode=1980JAP....51.3762D }}{{primary source inline|date=January 2025}}</ref> In late 1960s he launched a program based on combining semiconductors with magnetic ions, that started a new field of diluted magnetic ("semimagnetic") semiconductors (DMSs).<ref name=hjh/> These new materials revealed a host of novel phenomena, such helicon-excited spin resonance,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Holm |first1=R.T. |last2=Furdyna |first2=J.K. |title=Observation of helicon-excited electron paramagnetic resonance in a high-mobility semiconductor |journal=Solid State Communications |date=October 1974 |volume=15 |issue=8 |pages=1459–1462 |doi=10.1016/0038-1098(74)91402-1 |bibcode=1974SSCom..15.1459H }}{{primary source inline|date=January 2025}}</ref> a number of effects arising from modifications of semiconductor band structure by the presence of magnetic ions in the semiconductor lattice, such as spin-dependent forms of [[quantum oscillations]] in electrical transport and [[colossal magnetoresistance]] in [[P-type semiconductor|p-type]] [[Mercury (element)|Hg]]<sub>1-x</sub>[[Manganese|Mn]]<sub>x</sub>[[Tellurium|Te]], a host of novel magneto-optic effects (including giant Faraday effect),<ref name=whoosh/> as well as interesting magnetic phenomena, such as [[spin glass]] behavior<ref name=ttt/> and new forms of antiferromagnetic order<ref name=jmn/> (including helical and incommensurate In addition to work by Furdyna's team at Notre Dame on the DMS-based [[Quantum heterostructure|quantum structures]],<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Zeeman tuning of II–VI-based diluted magnetic semiconductor superlattices|first=J. ==Death==
Furdyna died on September 28, 2026, at the age of 93.<ref>{{cite web |title=Jacek Furdyna |url=https://www.palmerfuneralhomes.com/obituary/Jacek-Furdyna |website=Palmer Funeral Homes |access-date=2 October 2026}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
*Fellow, American Physical Society
*Fellow, American Association for the Advancement of Science
*Fellow, Institute of Physics, United Kingdom
*Fellow, Nanovic Institute of European Studies, University of Notre Dame
*2002 – Doctor of Science Honoris Causa, Warsaw University
*2007 – Doctor of Science Honoris Causa, Purdue University<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.purdue.edu/science/Alumni/recognition/honorary_doctorates/jacek-furdyna.html|title=Jacek K. Furdyna – College of Science – Purdue University|website=www.purdue.edu}}</ref>
*2009 – Nicholas Copernicus Medal, Polish Academy of Science<ref name="auto"/>
